summary: Specifies linear protection switching for MPLS-TP networks, supporting the capabilities of a packet transport network as defined by the ITU-T. It is a joint IETF and ITU-T effort and covers protection against failures along a path.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6378 explains how the two ends of an MPLS-TP connection coordinate a move to a reserved backup path when the working path fails. They send short status messages and use shared rules to settle on which path carries traffic.

subtitle: How two MPLS-TP endpoints coordinate a switch from a failed working path to a reserved protection path.

tldr.problem: When a transport path fails, both ends of a protected connection need to coordinate which path carries traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The Protection State Coordination (PSC) protocol sends status messages over the protection path. Each endpoint compares local alarms and commands with the peer's request, then follows defined state and priority rules.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6378 defines a single-phase coordination protocol for selected MPLS-TP protection arrangements. It recommends rapid initial messages to support switching within 50 ms and has been updated by RFC 7214, RFC 7271 and RFC 7324.

today: RFC 6378 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7214, RFC 7271 and RFC 7324. Read those updates together with this specification.

sections.title: Why Protection Needs Coordination
sections.content:
MPLS Transport Profile (MPLS-TP) networks use label-switched paths (LSPs) to carry traffic. Linear protection reserves a separate protection path for one or more working paths, so traffic can move when a failure or degradation occurs.

For a point-to-point path, the protection domain includes its two Label Edge Routers (LERs) and the paths between them. This RFC defines Protection State Coordination (PSC) messages so the endpoints can coordinate protection switching, especially for bidirectional paths.
sections.plainLanguage: A protected connection has a working path and a reserved protection path. The two endpoints use PSC to coordinate a change between them when a fault occurs.

sections.title: Protection Architectures in Scope
sections.content:
In 1+1 protection, a permanent bridge sends traffic over both paths and a selector at the receiving end chooses one. Bidirectional switching in this arrangement needs PSC. In 1:1 protection, traffic uses one path at a time, with selectors at both ends that must agree.

The basic protocol is designed for 1:1 protection and for 1+1 protection of a bidirectional path. It also permits coordination for unidirectional switching in a bidirectional 1+1 path. Use for 1:1 unidirectional protection, 1:n protection and point-to-multipoint paths is outside this document's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: In one arrangement, traffic is sent on both paths and the receiver chooses a copy. In another, traffic uses one path at a time, so both endpoints must coordinate their selectors.

sections.title: Local Triggers and Priorities
sections.content:
Local Request logic receives operator commands, server-layer alarms, control-plane indications, Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) indications, and signals from the Wait-to-Restore timer. It selects the highest-priority active local request and passes that request to PSC Control logic.

The control logic compares the local request with the request from the far endpoint and the current state. Operator commands include Lockout of protection, Forced Switch, Manual Switch and Clear. OAM must report detected failure or degradation to the local logic; Signal Degrade behavior is left for future specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Each endpoint considers alarms, operator commands and timer signals. It uses the highest-priority local request, then compares it with the message from the other endpoint before deciding what to do.

sections.title: Protection States and Recovery
sections.content:
The protocol tracks six protection-domain states: Normal, Unavailable, Protecting failure, Protecting administrative, Wait-to-Restore (WTR) and Do-not-Revert. In Normal, traffic uses the working path. In Protecting failure, traffic uses the protection path because the working path has failed; an administrative command can also move traffic to protection.

WTR delays reversion after a working-path failure has cleared, giving the path time to stabilize. In non-revertive operation, Do-not-Revert keeps traffic on the protection path until an operator directs a return. Each endpoint records whether its state came from a local input or a remote PSC message.
sections.plainLanguage: The endpoints track whether the connection is normal, unavailable, using protection, or waiting to return. After a fault clears, a timer can delay the return so an unstable path does not cause repeated switching.

sections.title: What a PSC Message Says
sections.content:
PSC messages travel in the MPLS Generic Associated Channel (G-ACh), using channel type 0x0024. The payload identifies the protocol version and request, the protection type, whether operation is revertive, the path with the fault or command (FPath), and the path carrying user data (Path); optional TLVs may follow.

The Request value names conditions such as Lockout of protection, Forced Switch, Signal Fail, Manual Switch, Wait-to-Restore, Do-not-Revert or No Request. For the basic protocol, the version is 1 and the TLV length is zero. Reserved fields must be sent as zero and ignored when received.
sections.plainLanguage: A PSC message reports what the endpoint detected and which path has the fault. It also says where user traffic is going, so the peer can make a matching decision.

sections.title: Sending Messages and Switching
sections.content:
The protocol is single-phase: an endpoint switches when its local rules require it and informs the peer without waiting for an acknowledgement. The endpoints can briefly select different paths while a message is in transit; the peer updates its state after receiving the message.

Messages are sent only over the protection path. After a local state change, the endpoint sends three messages as quickly as possible and then repeats its latest message. For switching within 50 ms, the RFC recommends that the first three messages be no more than 3.3 ms apart; the default continual interval is 5 seconds.
sections.plainLanguage: An endpoint switches first and tells its peer, without waiting for a reply. It sends the new message several times quickly, then repeats it periodically so the peer can catch up or detect that the session is still active.

sections.title: Security of PSC Messages
sections.content:
PSC relies on the security of the Generic Associated Channel and the broader MPLS security model. The RFC says changing a control message would generally require compromising a transit node, which it considers difficult and not something the protocol can prevent by itself.

Accidental corruption of the Request, FPath or Path fields could change peer behavior. The specified state transitions are designed to converge on stable behavior when a message does not match the actual condition. The RFC also notes that transit nodes should not police the associated channel.
sections.plainLanguage: PSC depends on the channel that carries its messages. A damaged message can affect switching, so the protocol defines state rules that settle into stable behavior even when a report does not match the fault.
